abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The combustion of lithium-ion batteries is characterized by fast ignition, prolonged duration, high combustion temperature, release of significant energy, and generation of a large number of toxic gases. Fine water mist has characteristics such as a high fire extinguishing efficiency and environmental friendliness. In order to thoroughly investigate the temperature control effect of fine water mist on lithium-ion battery fires. This study employs numerical simulation methods, utilizing PyroSim software to simulate the fire process in lithium-ion battery energy storage compartments. First, we focus on the variation patterns of flame, changes in combustion temperature, and heat release rate over time at environmental temperatures of 10, 25, and 35 °C. Subsequently, the suppression of flame, reduction in temperature, and changes in heat release rate are simulated for water mist in lithium-ion battery fires. The simulation results indicate that the environmental temperature has a considerable impact on the flame but a lesser effect on the heat release rate. Fine water mist effectively impedes the spread of thermal runaway between internal battery core cells, leading to a reduction in the flame size and a significant decrease in the maximum temperature and heat release rate. The numerical simulation results can provide scientific guidance for the prevention and control of fires in lithium-ion battery energy storage compartments.

sec.p: Received 2024 Jan 29; Accepted 2024 May 31; Revised 2024 Apr 3; Collection date 2024 Jun 25.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: With the advancement of society, electronic devices have experienced robust development, and lithium-ion batteries have emerged as a prominent choice due to their high volumetric and gravimetric energy density, long cycle life, low self-discharge, absence of memory effect, and environmentally friendly characteristics, along with a broad operating temperature range. Moreover, the excellent charge–discharge performance and low environmental impact of lithium-ion batteries align with the current global trend in the battery industry, emphasizing green and sustainable development as well as the ongoing pursuit of smaller, lighter, and more efficient batteries. In recent years, energy storage has garnered widespread attention,1 prompting many countries to incorporate lithium-ion batteries into energy storage systems. Originally applied in battery cells and capacity energy storage systems, lithium-ion batteries have progressively found applications in large-scale energy storage station systems for grid energy storage. However, despite the rapid development and extensive application, incidents of fires at energy storage stations have become more prevalent in various countries. Figure 1 presents a statistical overview of the occurrences of fires at energy storage facilities in recent years.

caption.p: Fire incidents at energy storage stations in recent years (from https://www.escn.com.cn/20231223/d098c998456d4e26b693db285bb6bb5c/c.html).

sec.p: Experts and scholars, addressing diverse fields and needs, have proposed and developed various energy storage technologies to meet human demands. Among these, lithium-ion battery energy storage technology stands out as the most feasible means. The development of lithium-ion batteries has progressed alongside advancements in materials science and intercalation science.2 As the share of new energy rapidly increases in the overall energy system.3,4 Lithium-ion battery energy storage technology has witnessed swift development in the field of new energy.

In recent years, both domestic and international scholars have increasingly dedicated their efforts to the study of lithium-ion battery fires. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in the United States conducted experiments on the heat release rate of lithium-ion batteries to determine factors such as combustion heat release, combustion time, and temperature.5 The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) conducted numerous fire simulation experiments to ascertain the fire characteristics of lithium-ion batteries.6−8 Meanwhile, researchers like Chen conducted thermal runaway experiments on the type of 18650 lithium-ion batteries with different charge amounts, observing experimental phenomena to study various characteristics of lithium-ion batteries after combustion.9−11 Sarkos focused on lithium-ion batteries with Licoo2 as the cathode material, analyzing the distribution of surface temperatures and studying changes in heat generation based on internal chemical reactions, variations in the discharge structure of lithium-ion batteries, and polarization phenomena during the reaction process.12 Sato examined heat generation during the charge–discharge process of lithium-ion batteries, deriving formulas for the source and magnitude of heat through analysis and verification.13 Hesse provided an overview of lithium-ion battery energy storage technology and its characteristics in terms of performance and aging. This analysis included a detailed examination of the storage system design based on evaluations of actual projects. Hesse proposed further research to fully exploit the potential of stationary battery energy storage systems, emphasizing the need for future studies to adopt a holistic system-level approach.14 Darcovich have studied the scenarios of electricity and cogeneration through simulation, and combine lithium-ion battery technology based on electrochemical fundamentals, treat transient battery charging and discharging.15 Chirkov have used computer simulation methods; the influence of the structure of the cathode active layer on the overall characteristics of lithium batteries during charging and discharging was elucidated. A series of obstacles in the process of improving the overall characteristics of lithium batteries were revealed.16 Wang et al. highlighted that the main causes of battery fires are combustible gases and electrolytes overflowing from safety valves. While agents like HFC-227ea can quickly extinguish flames, the intense chemical reactions within the battery may cause it to reignite. Wang reviewed thermal runaway phenomena and related fire dynamics in single lithium-ion cells and battery packs, discussing potential fire prevention measures.17,18 Zhang et al. utilized fault tree analysis and Bayesian network methods to assess the fire risk of Lithium-ion Battery Energy Storage Systems (LBESS) during maritime transport, calculating the probability of fire incidents during the transportation process.19 Liu et al. proposed a one-dimensional voltage-correlated convolutional neural network (1DVCNN) to detect and locate internal short-circuit faults in lithium-ion battery energy storage systems for timely diagnosis of faults.20 Dong established a comprehensive reliability assessment method for battery energy storage systems, considering both the health index of batteries and the impact of thermal runaway faults.21 Xu et al. based on the whole life cycle theory, developed an evaluation model for critical aspects of energy storage station construction and operation, providing a rational assessment of the benefits of lithium-ion battery energy storage stations on the generation side.22 Yang found that failure to promptly dilute combustible gas concentrations could lead to explosions initiated by combustible gases produced by individual battery modules through a study on the gas explosion risk of containerized lithium-ion battery energy storage stations.23 Sun and Wang conducted fire and extinguishing tests on Li/graphite electrodes, comparing the inhibitory effects of fire extinguishing agents on the propagation of thermal runaway in confined spaces.24 Ye et al. investigated the dynamic thermal behavior of overcharging batteries under adiabatic conditions, concluding that constant current-constant voltage-constant current overcharging is more dangerous than constant current overcharging.25 Xie et al. have used PyroSim software to simulate the fire scenario caused by thermal runaway of lithium-ion batteries stored in warehouses, the temperature change, heat release rate, visibility change, and CO volume fraction change around the fire ignition source.26 The aforementioned studies have seldom touched upon the temperature changes during the thermal runaway process of lithium-ion batteries caused by seasonal temperature variations. Moreover, the positioning of fine water mist fire extinguishing nozzles was often based on engineering practice experience, lacking systematic research.

In summary, this paper focuses on a lithium-ion battery energy storage facility, utilizing PyroSim software to establish a numerical simulation model for fire incidents. Initially, the study investigates the variation pattern of the thermal runaway temperature of lithium-ion batteries with different distances from the ignition source. It examined the cooling differences in the lithium-ion battery fire at the energy storage station caused by a fine water mist at various nozzle positions. Finally, the research explored the temperature control effects of fine water mist on lithium-ion battery fires at the energy storage station under different seasons and environmental temperatures (10, 25, 35 °C). The findings of this study provided scientific guidance for the prevention and control of fires in lithium-ion battery energy storage compartments.

sec.title: Theoretical Analysis
sec.p: PyroSim software is primarily based on computational fluid dynamics theory, simulating the distribution of smoke flow when the research subject experiences a fire. It predicts the concentration distribution of toxic and harmful gases as well as the temperature distribution of smoke during a fire using measurement points. The required computational formulas are as follows.
Mass conservation equation.
Momentum conservation equation.
Energy conservation equation.
Ideal gas equation.

sec.title: Model Creation
sec.p: When simulating calculations using PyroSim, this paper selected an energy storage compartment with dimensions of 20 feet (length: 6.058 m, width: 2.438 m, height: 2.591 m) as shown in Figure 2. The individual batteries chosen for this study were the brand Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), model CATL 280Ah, with dimensions of 173.9 × 207.2 × 71.7 mm. Other positions in the compartment were designated for distribution cabinets measuring 1.35 m in length, 0.8 m in width, and 2.3 m in height. Before modeling with PyroSim, it was necessary to define a computational domain within PyroSim. After the number of computational domains was determined, the next step involved partitioning the grids. In numerical simulation studies, grid density forms the foundation of simulation calculations and the accuracy of the simulation is closely tied to the grid density. Finer grid densities typically yield more accurate computational results. In this study, the precision of the fire source characteristics is commonly represented by D*/δx, where D* is the characteristic diameter of the fire source, and δx is the grid size. The calculation formula for D* is given below.

Q represents the fire source power in kilowatts (kW); ρ0 is the air density in kilograms per cubic meter kg/m3, commonly taken as 1.29 kg/m3; CP is the specific heat capacity of air in kilojoules per kilogram per Kelvin kJ/(kg K), typically considered as 1.005 kJ/(kg K); g is the gravitational acceleration in meters per second squared (m/s2), usually assumed to be 9.8 m/s2; and T0 is the ambient temperature in Kelvin (K), taken as 303 K in this case. In this simulation, a comparison was made for grid sizes of 0.03 and 0.05. Following a foundational simulation, the model was modified and improved based on the errors indicated by FDS. Finally, the grid dimensions were set at 0.05 × 0.05 × 0.05 m. The modified model was then subjected to simulation, and the grid construction is successfully completed.

sec.title: Fire Setting Scenario
sec.p: In this section, the research focused on the thermal runaway of batteries leading to fires and the impact of fine water mist on fire incidents in a containerized lithium-ion battery energy storage compartment. Given the symmetrical arrangement of batteries in the battery compartment, fire sources were placed in different positions to simulate various scenarios and temperature variations in the system were observed through simulations. The individual battery model used is the CATL 280A, operating under direct current. The battery operated in a temperature range of 0–55 °C under charging conditions and −30 to 55 °C under discharging conditions. Short-term storage was adaptable to temperatures ranging from −20 to 65 °C, and long-term storage was adaptable to temperatures from −20 to 55 °C. This study focuses on the temperature fluctuations within lithium-ion battery energy storage compartments across various seasons, as well as the temperature control efficacy of fine water mist in suppressing lithium-ion battery fires in energy storage stations. According to the data obtained from the local meteorological bureau in a central city of China, the average indoor temperature in winter is 6.8 °C, in spring and autumn it is 23.6 °C, and in summer it is 36.9 °C. Since the batteries in the lithium battery energy storage warehouse generate heat during operation, the temperature inside the warehouse will be higher than the room temperature. Therefore, we choose 10, 25, and 35 °C as the ambient temperatures for the working conditions. We established indoor temperature conditions of 10 °C for winter, 25 °C for spring and autumn, and 35 °C for summer. Therefore, environmental temperatures were set at 10, 25, and 35 °C, respectively. The fire suppression method chosen is the use of a fine water mist. As a fire occurs, the ambient temperature rapidly increases and stabilizes at a certain value. Therefore, activating the fine water mist system when the ambient temperature reached its maximum was crucial for effectively suppressing fires within containerized lithium-ion battery energy storage compartments.

The design steps include determining the positions of measurement points and slices, the location of the fire source, the location of water mist nozzle, the maximum heat release rate, and the environmental conditions. The location of the fire source was: X (0.469,0.6429) Y (1.7249,1.9321) Z (0.605,0.6767). The water mist sprayers were set above the center of the energy storage chamber, at the same height as the detector, to achieve a better fire suppression effect. Their locations were: (1.2, 1.22, 2.55), (2.4, 0.5, 2.55), and (3.4, 1.22, 2.55). To better reflect changes in fire sources at various stages, detection points for environmental temperatures needed to be set. Simultaneously, positions for temperature slices were required (See Figure 3), where the temperature slices including: X = 2.0 m Temperature; X = 4.0 m Temperature; Y = 0.5 m Temperature; Y = 1.5 m Temperature; Z = 1.0 m Temperature; Z = 2.0 m Temperature.

Setting up a steady-state heat source, choosing to establish a heat source, and monitoring its temperature is crucial. To accurately detect the temperature around the heat source, multiple thermocouples were incorporated into the model during its construction. These thermocouples helped us observe temperature variations in the environment surrounding the heat source under different scenarios. The positions of six environmental temperature detection points were (0.2, 0.5, 2.55), (2.2, 0.5, 2.55), (2.2, 1.5, 2.55), (4.2, 0.5, 2.55), (4.2, 1.5, 2.55), (0.2, 1.5, 2.55), (1.2, 0.5, 2.25), and (1.2, 1.5, 2.25). The positions of the heat source and detection points in the model were illustrated in Figure 4.

sec.title: Scenario Configuration
sec.p: During the simulation process, a total of four fire scenarios were established to investigate the temperature control effect of the fine water mist system on the lithium-ion battery energy storage compartment. The first scenario was set at room temperature (25 °C) to monitor the temperature when fires occurred at different locations. The main distinction among the three remaining scenarios lies in the varying ambient temperatures. All four scenarios incorporated a fine water mist system for comparative analysis. sec.title: Temperature Variation Patterns at Different Distances from the Heat Source
sec.p: At room temperature, an analysis was conducted of the temperature variation over time at different monitoring points in the lithium-ion battery energy storage compartment during a fire. The comparison of temperature variations and numerical values involved the following steps to select optimal observation points. Additionally, a fine water mist system was configured for comparative purposes as follows.

As shown in Figure 6, during a fire incident, the ambient temperature rapidly increased, reaching its peak after a certain period, and gradually stabilized. The temperature increased significantly at a location closer to the fire source (Detection Point 6#), reaching a maximum temperature of 340 °C; the maximum temperatures at Detection Point 1# and 8# reached 284 and 240 °C, respectively. As the distance from the fire source increases, the rate of temperature increases and the maximum ambient temperature decreases, with the highest temperature values measured at 2#, 3#, 4#, 5# and 7# which were far from the fire source, were all no higher than 150 °C.

caption.p: Temperature changes without the fine water mist system at room temperature.

sec.p: Examining the temperature variations at different positions from the fire source is depicted in Figure 7. Prior to activating the fine water mist system, temperatures experienced a rapid ascent across all locations. Once the ambient temperature reached its peak, the fine water mist system came into operation. With the cooling effect of the fine water mist, temperatures at various positions within the system commenced a descent. The rate of temperature decrease varies across different locations, the temperatures at 6# experiencing a more rapid decline, dropping to 210 °C within 400 s, while the temperatures at Points 1# and 8# decreased to 195 and 133 °C, respectively. In contrast, temperatures at Detection Points 2#, 3#, 4#, 5# and 7#, farther from the fire source, gradually decreased below 60 °C and eventually returned to room temperature after the fine water mist system was engaged.

caption.p: Temperature changes with a fine water mist system at room temperature.

sec.p: By comparing Figures 6 and 7, it was evident that the temperature variation was more pronounced at location 6#, and the temperature change at locations farther from the fire source was minimal after the fine water mist system was activated. To ensure comparability with the experimental group, subsequent data analysis would focus on the results obtained from 6#.

sec.title: Simulation Results Analysis at 10 °C
sec.p: Under the conditions of 10 °C ambient temperature, an analysis was conducted on the development of flames and the temperature variation over time during a fire in the lithium-ion battery energy storage compartment. Additionally, the impact of the fine water mist system on flames and temperature was examined after its activation. As shown in Figure 8, compared to the size of flames before the initiation of the fine water mist system, the flames were significantly reduced after the system had been operational for some time. At 400 s, the flame size with the fine water mist system in place was notably smaller than the flame without the mist system. The temperature curve was extracted from position 6#. After the occurrence of the fire, the ambient temperature rapidly increased and reached its peak at 260 s (310 °C). At this point, the fine water mist system started operating, exerting a suppressive effect on the fire, leading to a rapid decrease in ambient temperature. After 100 s of the fine water mist system operation, the ambient temperature gradually stabilized at 200 °C, significantly lower than the temperature without the fine water mist system.

caption.p: Temperature variation over time at an environmental temperature of 10 °C.

sec.title: Simulation Results Analysis at 25 °C
sec.p: Under the conditions of 25 °C ambient temperature, an analysis was conducted on the development of flames and the temperature variation over time during a fire in the lithium-ion battery energy storage compartment. Additionally, the impact of the fine water mist system on flames and temperature was examined after its activation. As shown in Figure 9, the changes in flames after the fine water mist system had been operational were similar to the conditions in scenario 2. The temperature curve was extracted from position 6#. After the occurrence of the fire, the ambient temperature rapidly increased and reached its peak at 250 s (330 °C). At this point, the fine water mist system started operating, exerting a suppressive effect on the fire, leading to a rapid decrease in ambient temperature. After 100 s of the fine water mist system operation, the ambient temperature gradually stabilized at around 210 °C, significantly lower than the temperature without the fine water mist system.

caption.p: Temperature variation over time at an environmental temperature of 25 °C.

sec.title: Simulation Results Analysis at 35 °C
sec.p: Under the conditions of 35 °C ambient temperature, an analysis was conducted on the development of flames and the temperature variation over time during a fire in the lithium-ion battery energy storage compartment. Additionally, the impact of the fine water mist system on flames and temperature was examined after its activation. As shown in Figure 10, the changes in flames after the fine water mist system had been operational were similar to the conditions in scenarios 2 and 3. The temperature curve was extracted from position 6#. After the occurrence of the fire, the ambient temperature rapidly increased and reached its peak at 240 s (340 °C). At this point, the fine water mist system started operating, exerting a suppressive effect on the fire, leading to a rapid decrease in ambient temperature. After 100 s of the fine water mist system operation, the ambient temperature gradually stabilized at around 225 °C, significantly lower than the temperature without the fine water mist system.

caption.p: Temperature variation over time at an environmental temperature of 35 °C.

sec.title: Maximum Temperature under Different Conditions
sec.p: Based on Figures 8–10, a comparison revealed the following insights regarding the maximum temperature reached and the flame height and width at 400 s: In scenarios without the fine water mist system, flames were larger when the initial ambient temperature is higher. Conversely, in scenarios with the fine water mist system, flames significantly decreased after the mist system was activated, indicating a substantial impact of the fine water mist system on the flame size. Comparing the time and numerical values for reaching the maximum temperature, in scenarios without the fine water mist system, a higher initial ambient temperature led to an earlier and higher peak temperature. In scenarios with the fine water mist system, the mist system was activated earlier due to the earlier peak ambient temperature.

As shown in Figure 11, during the 400s of combustion, as the fine water mist system operated for a period, the ambient temperature tends to stabilize. At the same ambient temperature, the maximum temperature reached in the environment without the fine water mist system was much higher than the stabilized temperature achieved with the mist system activated. With an increase in the initial ambient temperature, the maximum temperature without the fine water mist system rises and the stabilized ambient temperature after the mist system operates also increased correspondingly. In other words, a higher initial ambient temperature corresponded to a higher maximum temperature after a fire and a higher stabilized ambient temperature.

caption.p: System environment approaches a stable value under different conditions.

sec.title: Variation of Heat Release Rate under Different Temperature Conditions
sec.p: The heat release rate is the amount of heat released per unit of time under certain conditions during the combustion of a material. It is a crucial parameter reflecting the degree of fire hazard, and its numerical value indirectly determines the amount of smoke and the production of toxic substances during material combustion. In the PyroSim simulation, the heat release rate is a fundamental input parameter. In this study, the heat release rate per unit area was set at 3000 kW/m2, with the reaction material specified as “Burner”. The simulation focused on the scenario of a lithium-ion battery energy storage facility catching fire, and thus, the investigation into the heat release rate examined the influence of different temperatures under a fire heat release rate of 3000 kW/m2.

Figure 12 illustrates the trend in the variation of heat release rates, showing a generally consistent pattern among the three scenarios. The rates initially exhibited a gradual increase, followed by a sharp rise, with continuous fluctuations during the ascent. The times and corresponding values when the maximum heat release rates were reached under different ambient temperatures (10, 25, and 35 °C) are as follows: (266 s, 450 kW); (245 s, 449 kW); (222 s, 451 kW). It could be concluded that the maximum heat release rates under different ambient temperatures were comparable, but at higher ambient temperatures, the system reached the maximum heat release rate earlier.

caption.p: Time dependent heat release rate curves at different temperatures.

list-item.p: At the same ambient temperature, the flame size when the fine water mist system is activated is significantly smaller than the flame size when the mist system is not equipped. During a fire, the system temperature rises rapidly and stabilizes once it reaches a certain level. When the fine water mist system cools the environment above the flame, it tends to stabilize at a temperature significantly lower than the highest temperature reached without the mist system.

At different ambient temperatures, the flame size of the system with or without the fine water mist increases as the ambient temperature rises. The system reaches its maximum temperature earlier as the ambient temperature increases. With increasing ambient temperature, the maximum temperature reached by the system without the fine water mist also increases, and when the mist system is activated, the temperature at which it stabilizes also increases correspondingly.

The variation trend of heat release rate remains consistent across different ambient temperatures, with comparable maximum values of heat release rate. However, the time at which the maximum heat release rate is reached varies depending on the ambient temperature, with systems at higher ambient temperatures reaching the maximum heat release rate more quickly.
